key_terms.meaning: A central computer holds the part programs and feeds instructions to several NC machines one block at a time over a data link, replacing the punched tape reader.
Each machine keeps its own small computer and program memory; the central computer only downloads programs and collects shop-floor data.
The complete sequence of motion commands kept in the controller's memory (earlier on punched tape), so the same program can be run again without re-reading a tape.
A CNC machine with a rotating spindle that can mill, drill, bore and tap, using an automatic tool changer holding many tools.
A CNC lathe in which the work rotates and a turret of tools moves in X and Z, usually with a constant-surface-speed spindle.
The controller compares each commanded axis position with the position measured by an encoder and corrects the difference.
No position feedback is used; the controller sends a counted number of pulses to a stepper motor and assumes the slide reached the target.
Control in which two or more axes move together in a coordinated way so the tool follows a straight line or an arc while cutting.
Control that only guarantees the final position of each axis; the path taken between two holes is not controlled and no cutting happens during the move.
A hardware or software interpolator that adds small increments to each axis at every clock pulse, producing straight lines and arcs from simple additions.
The part of the CNC that handles on/off logic: coolant, tool change, pallet, doors, interlocks and machine safety signals.
A position sensor that reports the true position of the axis at power-on, because each shaft angle has its own unique code.
The machine-independent output of CAM software: the path of the tool centre in part coordinates, without any G codes or machine details.
A program that converts CL data into G code for one particular machine, respecting its axes, travels, speeds, tool-change codes and controller dialect.
The voltage across the tool-work gap in EDM; it rises until the dielectric breaks down and a spark flows.
The duration of one electrical discharge pulse in EDM, in microseconds; longer on-time removes more metal but leaves a rougher surface.
The radial gap, tool radius plus spark gap, by which the cavity produced in EDM is larger than the electrode.
A thin layer of melted and re-solidified metal left on an EDM surface, harder and more brittle than the parent metal.
EDM that uses a continuously travelling thin wire as the electrode, cutting through plates along a programmed path.
Cutting by a very fast jet of water carrying abrasive particles that erode the work, with no tool contact and very little heat.

takeaways: Numerical control moved the instruction from a punched tape to a computer memory, and DNC moved it from the machine to a central computer.
A CNC machine is a stiff structure with low-friction guideways, a spindle drive and a feed drive, all sized to hold position under cutting force.
The controller turns a wanted path into a stream of axis position commands and compares each command with the measured position, correcting the error.
Open loop with a stepper motor is cheap and suits light point-to-point work; closed loop with an encoder and servo is standard on contouring machines.
A part program is a list of blocks, and each block says where to go, how fast, and with what spindle speed and tool.
CAM software makes CL data from a CAD model, and a post-processor turns that CL data into G code for one specific machine.
EDM removes metal by repeated sparks across a dielectric-filled gap, so there is no cutting force and the electrode never touches the work.
Abrasive water jet machining erodes the work with a fast water jet carrying abrasive particles, giving a narrow heat-affected zone and no tool wear.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move from principle to sketch to parameter effect: a labelled block diagram, the defining equations or parameter names, and the practical consequence for accuracy, surface finish and tool life, with one Indian shop-floor example.

bank.q: Trace the evolution from NC to CNC and then to DNC. Distinguish direct numerical control from distributed numerical control.
outline: Punched tape NC: fixed logic, tape re-read every part, no memory
CNC: stored program in memory, editable at the machine, one machine per controller
Direct NC: central computer feeds blocks to many machines in real time
Distributed NC: central host only downloads programs; each machine has its own computer and memory
Advantages: less tape handling, program editing, program library, production data collection
Typical uses: job shops with many part variants

bank.q: Describe the main building blocks of a CNC turning centre and a machining centre: structure, guideways, spindle drive and feed drive.
outline: Machine bed and column: ribbed cast iron or welded steel, filled or polymer concrete for damping
Guideways: hardened box ways (friction, high damping) or linear recirculating-ball guideways (anti-friction, low stick-slip)
Spindle drive: DC shunt motor or AC induction motor with vector drive, gearbox or belt, constant surface speed
Feed drive: ball screw or linear motor, stepper or servo motor, encoder feedback
Tool turret and automatic tool changer, with tool storage and identification
Sizing: thrust and torque must hold position within a few micrometres under cutting force

bank.q: Explain open loop and closed loop control in CNC machine tools with block diagrams, and state where each is used.
outline: Open loop: controller to pulse counter to stepper motor to ball screw, no feedback
Error sources in open loop: lost steps, backlash, thermal growth
Closed loop: command compared with encoder measurement, error drives the servo amplifier
Elements: interpolator, position loop, velocity loop, current loop, tachogenerator and encoder
Choice: stepper for light, cheap, point-to-point; servo for contouring, heavy cuts, accuracy
Mention resonance, gain, and following error in contouring

bank.q: Explain point-to-point, straight-cut and contouring control systems with a sketch of the tool path in each case.
outline: Point-to-point: final position only, path irrelevant, no cutting during move, used on drilling machines
Straight-cut (paraxial): one axis at a time in motion, giving lines parallel to axes, used on simple milling
Contouring: two or more axes coordinated continuously, straight lines and arcs at constant feed
Interpolator types: DDA hardware, software, reference-pulse and sampled-data
Effect on surface finish and feed-rate limits

bank.q: Write a manual part program for a part with four holes on a rectangular pitch and one straight milled edge on a CNC machining centre. Explain each block.
outline: Program header: program number, absolute mode G90, units G21, work coordinate G54
Tool call and spindle start: T word, M06, S word, M03
Rapid to first position with G00, drill cycle G81 with R and Z depth
Repeat or use G91 incremental for remaining holes, or G52/G54 offsets
Cancel cycle G80, raise tool, stop spindle M05, end program M30
Explain each G and M code, feed F in mm/min, and safe Z height

bank.q: Explain circular interpolation by the DDA method. Show how a straight line from (0,0) to (6,4) is generated in a few clock pulses.
outline: Principle: accumulate an increment in one register, overflow in the other axis register produces a step
For a line, increments proportional to axis displacement, so both axes finish together
Table of clock pulse, accumulator value, carry, step taken, position
For an arc, start and end point plus centre or radius given; increments change sign at quadrant points
Result: small quantised steps approximating the straight line, chord error set by resolution
Mention hardware DDA versus software interpolation in the controller

bank.q: Describe computer-aided part programming. Show the flow from a CAD model to cutter location data and then to machine G code.
outline: CAD model: geometry, part features, tolerance
CAM: tool selection, machining strategy, cutting parameters, tool path generation
CL data: cutter location points in part coordinates plus tool axis and feed
Post-processor: converts CL data to a specific controller's G code using a machine configuration file
Simulation and verification, gouge and collision check
Advantages: complex 3-D surfaces, reduced programming time, standardised output
Partly spans manual programming: comparison with manual G-code writing

bank.q: Explain the working principle of die-sinking EDM. Describe the function of the dielectric, the servo-controlled gap and the main process parameters.
outline: Spark across a small gap in dielectric; melting and vaporisation of a tiny volume; crater formed
Tool is the cathode, work is the anode in the usual connection
Dielectric: kerosene or deionised water; flushes debris, cools, insulates until breakdown
Gap voltage builds until breakdown, discharge, recovery; servo maintains gap around a few tens of micrometres
Parameters: peak current, on-time, off-time, gap voltage, flushing pressure, electrode material
No cutting force, so thin sections and hardened steel can be machined; electrode wear ratio matters
Surface finish and recast layer depend mainly on energy per spark

bank.q: Explain wire EDM. How is the wire kept in tension and how is overcut compensated to obtain an accurate die opening?
outline: Thin brass or coated wire travels from a spool to a take-up reel, used once
Work is a plate mounted on a table; wire cuts a narrow kerf through it
Deionised water dielectric, flushing from top and bottom nozzles
Overcut equals half of kerf minus wire radius; tool path is offset by the wire radius plus gap
Multiple trim passes for finish and accuracy; corner control and taper cutting
Applications: press tool dies, punches, extrusion dies, hard conductive material

bank.q: Analyse how peak current, on-time and off-time affect metal removal rate, surface finish, wear ratio and recast layer in die-sinking EDM.
outline: Metal removed per spark grows with pulse energy, so MRR rises with peak current and on-time
Roughness rises with energy per spark: craters deeper and wider
Wear ratio worsens with long on-time and high current for a given electrode pair
Too short an off-time leaves debris in the gap, causes arcing and unstable cutting
Recast layer thickens with energy; may need finishing passes or post-machining
Trade-off: roughing with high current then finishing with low current

bank.q: Compare EDM and abrasive water jet machining with conventional milling on cutting force, tool wear, workpiece hardness, heat effects and accuracy. Then choose a process for cutting a 20 mm hardened tool steel plate with a curved profile.
outline: Force: near zero for EDM and AWJM, high for milling
Tool wear: electrode wear in EDM, abrasive nozzle wear in AWJM, cutter wear in milling
Hardness: EDM needs conductivity but not hardness; AWJM cuts almost any material; milling needs softer material and carbide tools
Heat: EDM leaves a recast layer, AWJM leaves a small heat-affected zone
Accuracy and finish: EDM tight with fine finish; AWJM has taper and wider kerf
Selection for the hardened conductive plate: wire EDM, with reasons
Spans both non-traditional chapters and CNC fundamentals of axis control

bank.q: A shop must make 500 deep square pockets in hardened die blocks and also cut thin sheets of composite. Evaluate which of die-sinking EDM, wire EDM or abrasive water jet machining should be used, and justify with process limits.
outline: Deep square pocket with sharp internal corners: die-sinking EDM with a shaped electrode; wire EDM cannot start a blind pocket
Electrode manufacture and wear allowance; number of electrodes for 500 parts
Composite sheet: non-conductive, so EDM is not possible; AWJM cuts it without delamination
AWJM taper and kerf, abrasives and nozzle life
Combination route: EDM for the die, AWJM for the composite trimming
Cost, cycle time and surface integrity reasoning

bank.q: Analyse the sources of positioning error in a CNC machine and explain how encoders, gratings and a laser interferometer are used to measure and correct axis position.
outline: Error sources: ball screw pitch error, backlash, thermal growth, guideway friction and stick-slip, structural deflection
Incremental encoder: pulse counting, needs a reference mark; absolute encoder gives position at power-on
Linear grating on the slide measures true table position, closing the loop past the screw
Laser interferometer: compares a laser wavelength with slide travel, used for calibration and compensation tables
Pitch error and backlash compensation stored in the controller
Distinguish machine accuracy from part accuracy under cutting load
Spans machine building and the control chapter

bank.q: Evaluate the claim that a closed-loop CNC machine is always better than an open-loop one for a small job shop in India facing frequent power cuts.
outline: Closed loop benefits: accuracy, contouring, heavy cuts, self-correction
Costs: servo motors, drives, encoders, tuning and maintenance
Open loop with stepper motors: cheaper, simple, but lost steps under overload
Power cut effects: position loss in open loop; absolute encoders or homing needed in closed loop
Work envelope, batch size, tolerance demanded decide the choice
Verdict depends on job mix, not a universal rule

glossary.def: Control of a machine tool by a coded set of instructions that give positions, feeds and spindle speeds.
Computer numerical control: an NC machine in which a dedicated computer stores and executes the part program.
The complete part program held in memory so it can be run repeatedly and edited.
The electronics and software of a CNC that read the program, interpolate the path and drive the axes.
The part of the controller that generates intermediate axis positions between two programmed points.
The motor, screw or linear motor and feedback that move a slide along one axis.
The motor and transmission that rotate the tool or work, often with constant surface speed control.
A screw with recirculating steel balls between screw and nut, giving low-friction, near-zero-backlash motion.
Lost motion when a screw or gear reverses direction, seen as a small position error on axis reversal.
A motor that turns a fixed angle for each input pulse, used for open-loop axis drives.
A motor with feedback that follows a commanded speed or position, used in closed-loop drives.
A sensor that converts axis position into a digital code, either incremental or absolute.
The ordered list of blocks of G and M codes that describes the tool path for a part.
One line of a part program, containing a sequence number, motion words, feed and spindle words.
A preparatory code that sets the mode of motion or a cycle, for example G01 straight feed or G81 drilling.
A miscellaneous code for machine functions such as spindle on, coolant on, tool change or program end.
The insulating fluid in EDM that breaks down at the spark gap, flushes debris and cools the cut.
The pause between two EDM pulses, in microseconds, during which the gap de-ionises and debris is flushed.
The maximum current of an EDM discharge, which sets the energy per spark and hence removal rate.
The ratio of electrode volume worn to work volume removed in EDM.
The width of the slot cut by wire EDM or by an abrasive water jet.
A hard, cheap mineral abrasive commonly used in abrasive water jet machining.
Building a part layer by layer directly from a CAD model, without a mould or cutting tool.
Rapid prototyping in which a laser cures a liquid resin layer by layer.
